newsitem.title: MEXICO: Ford again turns to Mexican plant to boost sales.
newsitem.headline: Ford again turns to Mexican plant to boost sales.

text.p: As it has in the past, Ford Motor Co. is turning to its landmark plant in the northern Mexican desert to boost flagging sales and give the automaker a new image.

The 1998 Ford Escort ZX2 Coupe, a sportier version of past Escort models, will be built exclusively in Hermosillo, about 165 miles (265 km) south of the Arizona border. The company was to launch the new model officially on Wednesday.

"They're kind of following a trend in the industry which is, one, to appear to the customer to be a fun company with a sporty car but, two, not to spend too much money doing it," said Lincoln Merrihew, an analyst with DRI/McGraw-Hill in Lexington, Mass.
"The Escort Coupe kind of satisfies both objectives."
This assembly plant is the same one that came as such a surprise to the automotive world after it came on line in 1986.
Although the Big Three had been building cars in Mexico for the local market for decades, it was the first plant built specifically for exporting to the U.S. market.
Ford chose to make its Ford Escort and nearly identical Mercury Tracer models here when the Big Three were still trying to overcome their image of making nothing but gas guzzlers.

"The Escort is in need of a makeover," said George Magliano of the WEFA Group in New York."It's gotten old and they're coming out with a redesigned, sportier version. They need to jazz up sales because it's been around a while and is suffering at the hands of the competition."

After the Escort became one of the top-selling cars in the United States in the 1980s, becoming the No. 1 passenger car one year, it slumped to No. 11 in 1996, with sales of 284,644 units, down from 285,570 in 1995. It trailed the Honda Civic/Del Sol, which had 286,350 sales in 1996, while the Chevrolet Cavalier gained ground with 277,222 sales in 1996, up from 212,767 in 1995.

"Maintaining that level of being among the top sellers makes you put out more effort because at the same time there are a lot eyes watching, more customers to satisfy," Plant Manager Jose Islas said. "It showed that a Mexican plant could go out and compete in the international markets."
During a recent tour of the plant, Ford workers appeared to be enjoying the new models, zipping out of the factory in the brand-new test vehicles, tires screaching as they lined up shiny new coupes.
Ford would not allow a Reuter photographer to photograph the redesigned Escort's picture, lest the competition get a premature look before the official unveiling.

Aside from being the pride of Hermosillo, a city of 900,000 whose economy in the past relied on agriculture and mining, the plant here has been a major success story for Ford, turning out 40 units per hour over two shifts, almost entirely for the U.S. and Canadian markets, Islas said.
Hermosillo makes the coupe and the Escort station wagon while Ford's plant in Wayne, Mich., makes the four-door Escort as well as the wagon on two shifts, producing 74 units per hour.
When Ford opened shop in Hermosillo, it created a new system of quality control by making each manager responsible for his area and allowing workers to solve problems directly.

Islas noted some small details, such as how he and others in management wear the same uniform as production line workers and how they all eat the same food in the same cafeteria. When Islas went to get coffee, he passed through a conference room where workers were holding a meeting. They joked and bantered with him instead of freezing in silence when the boss entered the room.
